review:
This is hands down the best detective game I have played. I love the noire style, and all the characters are well thought out and well written. There are a few problems with the core mechanics of the game, but they do not get in the way of the story. If you get Widescreen Fixer to fix the 30fps cap, the game will run like butter. I've only encountered one game breaking bug with Widescreen Fixer and it was in an optional side mission, and you can always just toggle it off at that point in the game. 

Pros:
-Great story
-Fun gameplay
-Good acting
-Likeable, well written characters

Cons:
-30fps cap without Widescreen Fixer, and even that isn't a perfect solution
-Some small, but noticable glitches

Overall: I definitely recommend this game, especially if you can pick it up on sale
4/5

L.A. Noire is a detective game, simple as that. If you're looking for another shoot everything rampage game like GTA just because this game is made by Rockstar then this is not the game for you. Sure there is shooting, but you won't be allowed to kill everyone in sight, running people over will affect your case rating etc.

[b] The Atmosphere	 [/b]
 Personally, I love the setting of the game, the late 40s jazz theme mixed with golden age Hollywood as well as a classic noir feel makes for a great mix, but while the storytelling is good, it's not all there. The story feels a bit like it's jumping around without finishing everything off, Rockstar gathered enough story for a movie, but not a 20 hour game. Because of this you will be left with extra things that feel like they are just there to fill up an hour of your time and parts of the story that are never properly concluded. This being said, the story has some great parts towards the second half of the game and does a great job 80% of the time, however the ending will feel incomplete. 

[b] Gameplay and Fun	 [/b]
It's fun to drive around and using your siren to move people out of the way is great. The car chases are exciting at first but end up being repetitive, as with all the chases. Shootouts feel this way too and there are one or two that will feel boring. The combat tends to feel stiff from time to time. For an open world game it is very linear and the free roam mode itself actually takes some working out to access. Street crimes are fun to attend to and interrogations are challeging. The clue finding in the game is brilliant and walking around the crime scenes never gets old although you will quickly work out the set structure to finding all the clues.

[b] Sound	 [/b]
The sound in the game makes for great immersion, no complaints here really. The hint sounds at crime sounds can be turned off if they make the game too easy and the whole feel of the sirens and the radio really sells the 40s atmosphere.

[b] Graphics	 [/b]
The facial expressions are the best part about the graphics, I didn't notice too many hiccups in the graphics and if I did they didn't distract from the game. The faces of people look incredibly lifelike and all the other graphics are good too. The sunny setting of Los Angeles adds a bright feeling to the game.

[b] Replayability	 [/b]
While you do have the option to replay your cases to get all clues and perfect your interrogation this game is likely to be one you will only play the story of once, it's still fun to drive around and do street crimes but the cases tend to be something that's best as a one time thing.

[b] Verdict	 [/b]
Overall this game is great fun and a nice step away from GTA while still keeping to the Rockstart format. It feels fresh but also familiar. The graphics look very good for a game that came out in 2011. You will feel very immersed in the time period through use of sound and surroundings. The open world side has something to be desired and Los Angeles doesn't exactly feel as alive as GTA 4's Liberty City or Watch Dog's Chicago, it doesn't have much of a personality, the characters do. If you're looking for a good open world game, this isn't it, if you're looking for a good story with a mix of puzzle and regular shoot/drive gameplay and well designed characters then this is it. 

Get this if:
[list]
    [*]You like a good story
    [*]You want diverse gameplay that makes you think
    [*]You like the Noir setting
[/list]
Don't get this if:
[list]
    [*]You want full freedom in an open world
    [*]You want to go on a killing spree
    [*]You don't care about story
[/list]
 [b] 8.5/10	 [/b]

Hearing the title L.A. Noire would first remind you the advance features that used in the game called motion scanned that give NPC's expression to make your interview feel as natural within reach. Also last thing but not the least, Starting the game would introduced you to a locked 30FPS, There's a fix here on [url=https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/L.A._Noire]PCGamingWiki[/url] called Widescreen fixed. [h1]ɢᴀᴍᴇᴘʟᴀʏ:[/h1]
The game mainly revolve a lot on the Interrogation part and finding clues which helps you connect the leads and nails the right question. It looks complicated at the start, But the things is, The choices [b]Doubt[/b] and [b]Lie[/b] is just the same. Picking Doubt is just another form of telling them they're lying, but without you having proof.

Just beat the game so these thoughts are fresh:

-You should avoid the PC version if you can. Not only do you have to download the stupid Rockstar launcher, there are also major performance issues (and this is coming from someone with a top end modern rig). This is especially odd since the game is locked to *gasp* 30 FPS. There are apparently fixes, and even ways to uncap the FPS, but they've got mixed reviews so I never bothered. I prefer PC gaming pretty heavily so I put up with it, and it was still playable, but if it's all the same to you, get the console versions.

-The facial animations in this game are genuinely incredible, and it shocks me that no game since has used them. I'm sure it was expensive as hell to do, but man, the game is worth playing for this alone. It just completely levels up the production value to another degree.

-Except for some forgivable game-y moments, the setting is extremely believable and impressively historically accurate. I loved the attention to detail. Passionately done.

-The first half of the game (ESPECIALLY the homicide desk) is so, so much worse than the second half. To the point that I was having a hard time getting myself through the game. I'm glad I did, because the final stanza is some of the best Adventure gaming I've ever played, but it saddens me that so many players don't make it that far (look at the achievements ... only 10-15% of players make it to the final 5 cases. Most quit long before that). Some of it is just fluff, and honestly the game would be better without it. This isn't so dissimilar to the 40 "street crime" sidequests; just an absolute waste of time that you -know- someone pushed for just to pump up the game's length. 

-The more the game drifts from its awesome writing and acting to well, being a game, the worse it is. You'll rotate through like 5 different gameplay segment types (driving, hand to hand combat, stealth, footchases, and 3rd person cover shooting). All of them are pretty bad, some embarrassingly so. The shooting is the one that's done the most, and I guess it's serviceable. You regen health. You take cover. You mow down 40 guys with a pistol as you shrug off hundreds of bullets because well you know what, it's a video game and you wanna get back to the good part: the story.

-Unfortunately the gameplay mechanics behind the adventure game sections (interrogations, investigations) might actually be worse. You spend a ton of time scouring for clues, but most of them go unused. And boy oh boy do some of the interrogation dialogue trees not make sense at all. Ugh, the interrogations. They're so bad. If you choose wrong in an interrogation, the game simply moves on, and you miss parts of the story (..terrible!). The game even does a little audio cue to let you know if you missed it (which bums you out every time). The end result is that after every case, I'd just go on Youtube to watch the parts I missed. And you know what, this game might genuinely be better on Youtube than as a game. I love visual novels, adventure games, etc. I get that the bar for gameplay isn't as high for this genre. But this here is a case of the gameplay getting in the way of the story, to the point that you actually miss parts of the story because of a very silly and poorly designed interrogation minigame.

LA Noire is a flawed game. It's not going to be for everyone, especially for people who don't love story-rich Adventure games. But I do. And I'll put up with a lot when a game this unique comes around. And that's the bottom line: there's nothing like LA Noire. Like, nothing is even close. There may never be another game like this. The amount of work required for the facial animations alone may mean we never see that tech again -- its been a decade since LA Noire came out and I can't think of another game that has used it since. And really, is another studio going to put 7 years into developing a high production value Adventure game with a noir setting? LA Noire might be a once in a lifetime game. And that alone makes it worth playing, warts and all.

There are games you know when you play that there hasn't been any real work put into it and most of the budget went into marketing. But there are some games that when you play, you KNOW that the sheer amount of creativity put into it and the expenses made to craft the experience and make a world has paid off.

And then there's LA Noire.

This game sets a new standard for the storytelling experience in games, not only with it's technology, but with it's excellent integration of good gameplay mechanics and using that as a way to unravel for yourself the world and it's mysteries.

The gameplay involved in solving the cases is pretty solid, with you scouting for clues that will later be used in interrogations. Though the clue-hunting is little more than a game of click-everywhere-until-something-happens, the meat is in the driving sequences and the interrogations. The driving sequences make full use of the fact that there's a big open world out there and anything could happen. Simply driving from one place to another is a nice experience as you see in full glory the love and patience with which Team Bondi recreated 1940s LA. Of course these can be skipped but you'll be missing out on the side missions which dot the city from time to time and can only be discovered if you take over the wheels.

But the true flavor comes from the interrogations. They used this technology masterfully in order to not only make the interrogations engaging, but also accessible with some exaggerations on the part of the actors which was done on purpose knowing full well the limitations this technology could have. Simply reading the expressions isn't enough since you also have to back up your accusations with evidence. This requires some thought and patience on your part and you need to read the descriptions of each clue carefully before using them. Suffice it to say that the game is worth it for these sequences and there are a LOT of them.

The story too is quite excellent with many noire elements, plot twists and an overarching conspiracy. LA Confidential, the 1997 movie set in around the same time, was a considerable influence for the game.

There are a few negatives though. Some cases felt like I wasn't really solving them. Even though ALL the cases have definitive culprits, there were a couple of cases where I felt I was simply going through the motions. The shooting isn't very good. The chase sequences on foot aren't really great as there are some navigation issues. Though the game is HUGE with MANY cases and the DLC also contributing to the list, there's not much to do outside the story missions which somewhat ruins the fact that these guys toiled so much to recreate this beautiful city. The PC port, though it has many of the features other PC ports lack like a good options menu and reasonable mouse support, it still is quite wonky though I wasn't too distracted by it.

Minor faults don't bring down this excellent game though. It is something I would definitely recommend to any gamer who wants to play a linear story-driven non-action intensive game. Suffice it to say that after I was done, I missed the game and felt just a little hollow inside.

[h1]TL;DR? See Conclusion[/h1]

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
L.A. Noire is an open world neo-noire police / detective game made by Team Bondi and published by Rockstar Games. It features crime scene investigation, interrogations, arrests, and possibly, for the first time in the Rockstar games portfolio, police chases where the player is the police.

If you like movies such as L.A. Confidential (specially this one), Chinatown and The Untouchables, you'll definitely might want to give this game a try.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Facial Animation: -The selling point of L.A. Noire is possibly the facial motion capture technology that was employed. It is this technique that makes the game's interrogations as close to realism as possible for the 'truth / doubt / lie' mechanic to work.

+ Atmosphere: -The devs have done remarkable work recreating the wonderful city of 1947 Los Angeles. Although it may not be exactly how it was back then, it's still a large and magnificent city to explore. From the cars, the clothing, the buildings and the radio, Team Bondi certainly nailed the 1947 atmosphere.

+ Investigation: -From examining clues to following leads, LA Noire delivers a great police / detective mechanic that provides fun and exciting experience.

+ Sound: -Great voice acting, great selection of 1940s classic hits, a bit of radio news from that time, good sound effects and some very classical OST vibe. The voice acting makes for some very memorable characters with unique personalities.

+ Playtime: -The game is extensive and will require some time to finish. From the main story, DLC cases, Street Crimes and Collectibles, there are a lot of things to do which is more than enough to make you feel that your money was well spent.

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- 30 FPS: -According to the devs, the reason for this was that the motion-capture technology would not function properly if it was not locked at 30 FPS. Be that as it may, most PC gamers would still expect certain games to run at 60fps minimum.

- Awkward Body Movements: -I kinda feel they focused a bit too much on the facial animation and severely under developed the body animation. Most character movements are awkward and the bodies seem to move like they were made from cardboard or cement.

-  No reward for Non-Lethal Arrest: -The game has optional 'Street Crimes' which can be solved by lethal or non-lethal methods (depending on the Crime). Unfortunately, there is no reward in trying to chase down a fleeing suspect and it would be much easier just to shoot them in the back. This disappointed me a lot.

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
GOOD GAME for a GOOD PRICE. L.A. Noire captures the classical 1940-70 police / detective movies that once graced the silver screens but with a bit of modern sprinkles to it. 

[h1]WORTH IT?:[/h1]
Sale or full price, this game is worth every penny.

I suggest that potential buyers of this game purchase the 'Complete' Edition which includes the DLCs because they extend the gameplay by providing additional 'Cases' for each of the game's chapters.

While this is an amazing concept for a game, it's harmed by several major issues.
1. Open world mechanics that contradict themselves - you can drive around in an open world, but you have to be very careful in a car that handles... poorly, or you get penalized. Not much fun, and there's nothing much of interest to find outside of the main cases - "street crimes" are boring "hold Y to catch perp" events.
2. Moon logic interrogations - the game has a poorly-explained, but somewhat consistent interrogation system in which you respond to statements by either believing them, doubting them or accusing them of being lies. The main cue for this is reading facial expressions, which I found to work mostly ok (but which went completely off-kilter every so often). The problem arises when the game assumes you mean something very specific which isn't clear a priori - what EXACTLY does my main character believe/doubt? If you fail to divine this, you'll be getting a lot wrong. It gets a lot worse when accusing, as the game then requires you to back your accusation up with some evidence chosen from the list of game-recognized evidence that you have found. Unfortunately, it's extremely unintuitive what the game will allow here. For example, in one case, I was questioning a witness who had seen some car thieves. Examining the car had earlier yielded that the license plates and a wheel were missing, but the witness said the car thieves had only gone for the wheels. So I check my notebook, which lists the evidence "missing license plate", and accuse him of lying. My character asks whether the witness is sure he didn't steal the plates himself, and I am prompted for evidence. I enter "missing license plate" - the witness absolutely just lied to me, as either the thieves took the plates OR the witness did. But no, apparently this isn't enough. It's WEIRD. Of course this evidence isn't conclusive - somebody else could have taken the plates while the witness wasn't looking, the witness might not have noticed the thieves also taking the plate and so on. But if the game requires this degree of granularity for proving a lie, then half of the interrogations before shouldn't have worked (this is about halfway through the game). Or was I supposed to show evidence that the WITNESS took the plates? It's inconsistent and frustrating.
3. The game wants you to be a perfectionist, but is designed to prevent it. You get audio cues during interrogations that tell you whether you were right or wrong, the game rates your performance each case and there's even a "rank" system that levels up with more "correct" cases solved. But at the same time, there's no quicksave and you have to restart a case from the beginning if you get something wrong - and the cutscenes are unskippable. If the game weren't so frustrating about getting interrogations right due to issue #2, this might not be so bad in a "live-with-your-decisions" kind of way, but as is, you feel cheated because you got something wrong and it seems arbitrary, but you can't do anything about it without sitting through cutscenes that were only marginally interesting the first time.

Really great ideas and perhaps worth a look just for that reason, but I feel the execution fails.

I beat the main story a long time ago, but finally got around to getting all achievements.  This is a detective story where you need to search for clues, interrogate suspects, victims, and witnesses, and decide if what telling you is the truth, doubtful, or a lie.  If you choose that it is a lie, you need to use the clues that you found to confront them with the truth.  You do this for 21 cases spread across a variety of police investigations.  You do traffic, homocide, arsen and more types of cases.  There is an overarching storyline that does follow these cases, though not always directly connected, but the game offers a compelling story.

The era is set in the late 40s post WWII.  You are Cole Phelps, a veteran who has come home and joined the LAPD.  The game is an open world, very similar to GTA with a beautifully rendered Los Angeles of that era.  There are a variety of cars for you to drive as well as trucks.  You can follow the main storyline or drive around searching for film reels, badges, street crimes, and collecting every single car available in the game.

One of the things that stands out in this game is the characters faces.  The technology used for this game is unique where actual actor's faces were used for great facial animation.  This facial animation technology was used to help you decide if someone is lying, telling the truth, or just not wanting to answer.  You can see this in their expression, the way their eyes look away when they tell a lie, or the face not matching the words that they are saying.  It's actually a pretty cool technology.  It doesn't look great by today's standards of graphics, but the facial expressions seem more advanced than what you see typically even today since they put so much effort in showing how characters react to questions.

The game is not difficult at all, the difficulty is trying to find all of the clues and guessing correctly on 1. Truth 2. Doubt 3. Lie when a character responds to your questions.  Also, due to the lifelike facial expressions, as per usual for Rockstar, the voices are great too.

The car radios offer some great 1940s commercials, music, and commentary, and just overall the sounds of the entire game is great even the sounds of the streets.  It took me some time to finish all of the achievements as the collection of items can be quite difficult on such a large map, but it was fun as the game offers a great atmosphere to explore and drive around in.

If you haven't played this game yet, I would definitely pick it up as it's a classic in the list of games that Rockstar has created.  Highly recommended.

L.A. Noire is, probably, one of the most expensive puzzle/investigative games ever made, and it shows. If you have watched films like L.A. Confidential and Chinatown, and consider them between your favourites, you cannot go wrong by playing L.A. Noire. That said, the game is far from perfect: the pacing of the main story is not good unfortunately. Also, due to the rushed nature of the development, they had to remove parts of the game that would have made the motivations of some characters much more believable. In general, the game is kind of repetitive, so I don't recommend binging it. Just play one or two cases per day, take breaks between each new promotion, and you will be fine.

All in all, L.A. Noire is quite a unique game, as nothing has come close to even try doing the same thing with this kind of scope. Even with all its drawbacks, L.A. Noire is for sure a game worth experiencing.

Well, there has been some time since I've played a game this intriguing. L.A. Noire is more like a classical 'noir' movie rather than a computer game, and you get to play the star of the movie! The storyline centers a young, promising police officer -later detective- named Cole Phelps in 1940s Los Angeles. His tale has everything: crime, murder, trauma, love, politics, justice, conflict of interest and ethics... mostly conflict everywhere.

The atmosphere is magnificent, graphics are more than satisfying and story builds around many twists and turns, always keeping you wondering about what might come next. The investigation process is well displayed, heavily depending on observation, whether it be a mimic of a suspect, or a tone in the witness' voice. The environment is wast and it is possible to get lost if you're not following the map indicators. You carry the full option of roaming the streets of L.A. to hunt for all kinds of achievements, and even venture out to solve trivial street crimes. I once again agreed that Rockstar never abstains from investing in environment design.

Controls of the game is a bit hard to master in PC though, I think this game is better suited for PS or Xbox in that manner. Vehicles are impossibly hard to control - at least for me, but my reflexes were never that great so I'm not the one to have a final call on that -  and that would be the sole minus for me that I've observed so far. I found myself preferring my partner to drive rather than myself, and that's a bit disappointing. Oh, well: I'm not in for the perfection anyhow.

I recommend it with CAPITAL CHARACTERS; for the story, graphics and display altogether.

L.A. Noire is a kind of game that we need more of. It isn't perfect by any means, but being a detective in 1940s Los Angeles is a hell of a premise for story and gameplay. I do hope we get a "sequel" for this game someday, maybe set in 80s Miami?

First, I want to get the bad things out of the way, because there are some frustrating this in this game (which can be pretty long). The drives from place to place can be too long, with not enough banter between your and your partner to fill up the silence and repetitive nature of driving. There's also no radio stations to choose from to listen to some 40s music or a good radio show, maybe even hearing about the events of the game on the radio, similar to how GTA series does it.
Additionally, the traffic is abhorrent; cars will almost intentionally get in your way, it's like they are programmed to get in your lane right when you get close to them. You can alleviate this by turning on your police siren, which makes the cars stop or get out of your lane, but that gets annoying pretty quickly.
The clues you find can sometimes be too vague when you accuse a suspect of lying, which can damage your case. Additionally, the car chases are too "on-rail"; enemy cars do not obey the law of physics and will follow a strict path no matter your influence, which can get frustrating quickly.
Furthermore, the game is a bit on the long side, with endgame cases being kind of a drag.

However, what the game does right is the story and its investigative gameplay. You go from an ordinary police officer to being promoted to Detective, with various desks, such as Traffic, Homicide, Vice, etc. There are some pretty cool storylines, a serial killer, shady corporate businesses, etc.
The 1940s atmosphere is authentic; the cars, the clothes, the way people behave and think, the music, everything is well done. The facial expressions are really great - the game gets memed on for the technology they used for mo-cap and facial expressions, resulting in some exaggerated expressions, however, most of the time the expressions are believable, almost like watching a noire TV show, since they were all scanned from real-life actors, most of which you will recognize.

All in all, I'd recommend this game to anyone who's interested in, but be aware of its flaws!

L.A. Noire is one of the best detective games ever created, and I cannot recommend it highly enough. The game takes place in the 1940s in Los Angeles, and the level of detail and authenticity is simply breathtaking. The voice acting is exceptional, and the facial animations are so realistic that you can easily read the emotions on characters' faces during interrogations.

The storyline is gripping and immersive, with plenty of twists and turns that keep you on the edge of your seat. And the open-world gameplay allows you to explore the city and investigate crimes at your own pace, which is a refreshing change from the linear gameplay of many other games in the genre.

It's worth noting that L.A. Noire is an older game, and as such, it may require some optimization to run properly on modern hardware and operating systems. I highly recommend checking in the game's Steam community hub for information on how to optimize the game for your system.

Overall, L.A. Noire is an absolute must-play for fans of detective games, crime dramas, or just great storytelling in general. If you haven't played it yet, do yourself a favor and pick it up today. You won't be disappointed!
